judgments.rationale: The frequency table supplies the probability and expected-value calculations; the demand estimate then applies that probability to the visitor total.
The mark scheme reduces the equation to a quadratic in sin x and then filters solutions in the stated radian domain; this is the trigonometric-equation method.
The exponential substitution produces a quadratic in e^x; the discriminant condition and k>0 give the required range.
The period identifies m and the remaining marks require a transformed sine-graph sketch with scale, amplitude, intercepts and extrema.
The area formula for an equilateral triangle is differentiated with respect to its changing side length; the geometric triangle relation is a separately used setup.
The given non-real factor, its conjugate root, and the remaining roots are determined with complex-number root relations; the existing geometry and probability labels are unrelated.
Reflecting f(|x|) and determining the range of its square use graph transformations; no separate inverse-function method is marked.
The spherical-ring volume is set up and evaluated by integration, then solved for h; the diagram only supplies the integration geometry.
The bearing angles and the sine rule solve the single triangle; no independent radian or identity technique earns marks.
Arc length, sector/triangle area and trigonometric geometry are assessed in (a)-(b), while integrating the rain-entry rate over 60-second periods is separately assessed in (c).

Parts (a)-(b) award marks for integrating the continuous density; parts (c)-(f) use independent-trial/binomial probability and explicitly count consecutive arrangements, so Integration and Counting and combinatorics are both material.
Euler approximation, implicit derivatives, Maclaurin terms and the exact differential-equation solution are all calculus methods; the series is not a Number-and-algebra sequence.
Composition is required in (a) and the graph sketch with extrema/endpoints in (b); differentiating to obtain extrema is not required by the mark scheme.
The marks assess fitting the x-on-y regression and using it for prediction, which is descriptive/regression inference rather than a function-inverse task.
The IQR identifies quartiles and the inverse-normal calculation determines the standard deviation; both normal distribution and descriptive statistics are used.
The required terms of both expansions and the resulting simultaneous equations are binomial-expansion work.
De Moivre powers, arguments and the Argand-plane rotation are handled within the complex-number method; the rotation is not a separate function transformation.
The line and plane direction/normal vectors and the angle formula are the marked work; trigonometric manipulation is subordinate to the vector method.
The proof assumes the contrary and derives an even/odd contradiction by algebraic parity, matching Proof and induction in the controlled taxonomy.
Integration by parts, a limit via l’Hôpital and numerical integrals dominate the calculus work; the final eight-mark proof explicitly uses induction.
AM-GM and integer optimization form the main algebraic work; later logarithm and derivative analysis are independently marked calculus components.
The arc length, perimeter and sector-area formulas are the entire marked method, with the angle measured in radians.
The circle/triangle coordinates provide an independently assessed setup, and differentiating the area expression supplies the maximum condition.
Complex polar form, De Moivre powers and polynomial-root transformations are all part of the complex-number method; no separate quadratic skill is required.
The antiderivative is obtained by substitution and integration by parts, then the interval areas are expressed as a sequence; the extra trigonometry label is not independently marked.
The asymptotes, intercepts and sketch are features of a transformed rational-function graph; no inverse-function method is assessed.
The area under the curve is evaluated by substitution/integration and logarithm laws; the displayed curve is not a graph-transformation task.
The variable is continuous uniform on [a,3a] and the variance calculation requires an integral; discrete-variable and inverse-function labels are unsupported.
The intersection identity, perpendicular tangent gradients and quadratic solution are marked; differentiation is an independently assessed tangent-gradient method.
The regression line is fitted and evaluated at d=20; this is descriptive regression work rather than an inference test.
The cosine model, period/amplitude and threshold times dominate; the random-time event probability is a separately assessed probability model.
The box draws are modeled by products of conditional probabilities; the mark scheme does not require a separate combinatorial count skill.
Euler’s method, separation and the exact solution of the stated equation are the central assessed methods; supplied derivative work supports the differential-equation analysis.
The cosine rule (or equivalent right-triangle setup) determines the angle, then sine gives the height; this is triangle geometry.
Parts (a)-(c) use normal probabilities and inverse normal, while part (d) explicitly uses a binomial model for ten bags; Discrete random variables is therefore materially assessed.
Acceleration-zero and rest conditions use differentiation, while distance over the sign-changing velocity interval is found by integrating velocity.
The line is verified from plane equations and the nearest point is found with vector/distance methods; graph transformations are not assessed.
The range uses a discriminant and part (b) solves a rational inequality after determining the sign of cos(t); function-inverse and trig-identity methods are not marked.
Graph comparison is primary; logarithm laws and derivative/tangent conditions are independently assessed secondary methods.
The defining arithmetic-sequence conditions and quadratic-root relationships are used throughout the question.
The stationary-point proof uses the derivative and its sign/values to classify extrema and relate them to x-axis intersections; this is an application of differentiation.
The orthogonal-family derivation solves a differential equation, with differentiation used to obtain the gradient relations.
Logarithm laws establish the quadratic, and discriminant/root analysis determines the parameter range and root separation; graph transformation is not marked.

Stationary-point classification and graph behavior use differentiation; the Maclaurin expansions use Limits and series; part (e) also evaluates a definite integral, requiring Applications of integration.
The complex binomial expansion and De Moivre identity are the central methods; the later polynomial manipulation is part of that complex/trigonometric derivation.
Union and complement rules determine both probabilities; no conditional-probability calculation is required.
Substitution of the complex number and equating real and imaginary parts (or equivalent root work) is the complete assessed method.
Both parts use integration by parts; logarithm laws are additionally needed to simplify the definite result.
The limit is evaluated by l’Hôpital’s rule or a Maclaurin expansion; the evenness proof is only a short symmetry step.
The 3D distance and angle in triangle BVC use vectors and cosine-rule methods; coordinates are input data, not a separate analytic-geometry method.
Normal quantiles determine the plant model, binomial probabilities handle the counts, and part (c)(ii) explicitly requires conditional probability.
Asymptotes, intercepts, graph sketch and range are function-graph work; the final inequality is independently solved and earns its own algebraic method.
The periodic exponential model is sketched and transformed, with the threshold event probability calculated at a random time.
Rest is found by differentiating displacement, and total distance is obtained from velocity integration while accounting for the direction change.
The discrete distribution’s total probability and expectation equations determine the parameter; solving the resulting cubic is part of that model method.
The variance formula for a binomial variable and the variance scaling rule for Y are the assessed discrete-random-variable methods.
The cross product is the central four-mark vector method, and the final area is one half of its magnitude; both vector and triangle-area methods are assessed.
Euler’s method and solving the first-order differential equation are the only central methods; the error is a direct comparison.
The logarithm laws produce the quadratic and its discriminant/root calculation determines the allowed parameter and root separation.
Stationary-point classification and graph behavior use differentiation; Maclaurin expansion and the definite integral approximation use calculus series/integration methods.
The complex binomial expansion and De Moivre identity drive the derivation; the equation-solving steps remain part of that complex/trigonometric method.
Union and complement rules determine both probabilities; conditional probability is not separately assessed.
Substitution and equating real and imaginary parts solve the complex equation; generic algebraic manipulation is too broad.
Integration by parts is required, and logarithm laws independently simplify the definite expression.
The limit condition is solved by l’Hôpital’s rule or a Maclaurin expansion, while evenness is only a short symmetry proof.
The 3D distance and angle in triangle BVC use vectors and cosine methods; coordinate notation is not an independent assessed topic.
